questions.q: Why does this lesson say a design that only exists as reasoning an architect can explain out loud isn't actually reviewable yet?
options: Because a reviewer who wasn't present for that reasoning needs a document that carries the decision and its reasoning on its own, without requiring the architect to explain it live
Because verbal explanations are always inaccurate
Because review boards never ask the architect any questions
Because Salesforce requires all architecture decisions to be stored in a specific database
questions.explain: A reviewer needs a document that stands on its own. If a design only exists as something the architect can explain verbally, it hasn't yet been put into a form a reviewer can actually evaluate independently.

questions.q: What is an Architecture Decision Record (ADR), as this lesson defines it?
options: A legal contract between two integrated systems
A diagram showing every object in a Salesforce org
A short, structured document capturing one specific decision, its context, and its reasoning, written at the time the decision is made
A record of every API call an integration has made historically
questions.explain: An ADR is a structured, written-at-decision-time document for one specific decision -- its context and its reasoning -- so a later reviewer doesn't have to reconstruct the thinking from memory or a live conversation.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what makes an ADR's "alternatives considered" section one of the most important, and most often shortchanged, parts of the document?
options: It's unimportant and can safely be skipped in most ADRs
It has to honestly name real alternatives and the reasons they were rejected -- an ADR with no real alternatives, or only strawmen, reads as a decision never actually tested against anything
It should only ever list alternatives that are obviously worse, to make the final decision look stronger
It is the only section a review board actually reads
questions.explain: Alternatives considered has to represent real options honestly, including why they lost. An ADR that lists no genuine alternative, or only an obvious strawman, signals the decision wasn't actually tested against serious competition.

questions.q: What test does this lesson give for whether an ADR's alternatives section was written honestly?
options: Whether it is longer than the "Decision" section
Whether it avoids naming any specific alternative design at all
Whether it was written after the decision was already implemented in production
Whether someone who disagrees with the final decision could read it and feel their position was represented fairly, even though it lost
questions.explain: The test is whether a disagreeing reader would feel fairly represented even in losing the argument. An alternatives section written just to make the chosen design look obviously correct by comparison fails that test.

questions.q: In the Meridian Fixtures ADR example, what does this lesson say the "Consequences" section should include?
options: What the decision makes easier and harder going forward, including that the two-pattern design is more complex to monitor and would need revisiting if catalog data ever needs to be more current than nightly
Only positive outcomes of the chosen design, with no mention of added complexity
A complete list of every Salesforce object touched by the integration
The exact dollar cost of building the integration
questions.explain: Consequences names both the tradeoffs accepted (added monitoring complexity from having two patterns) and what would trigger revisiting the decision later (a future need for more-current catalog data) -- not just a one-sided list of benefits.
